utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Thank you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Marela Jevtovic and Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Mr. Ackerman, at some point in time during the day on a piece of paper just jot down for me the dates when the Orthodox celebrate Christmas and epiphany because I know that they do not coincide with the Roman -- yes, but I need 13th and 14th January, what does it mean? Just put down on a piece of paper Christmas on such-and-such a date, epiphany on such-and-such a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will get the whole thing for you, Your Honour, in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there must have been an error, but I want to make sure that I'm right in the Scheduling Order, about dates. The Trial Chamber will sit instead of next week on Wednesday, the 20th and Thursday, the 21st of November. The Trial Chamber will sit on Friday, the 23rd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. 22nd. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm no confused now with all the series of dates. I thought I had better confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's obviously a mistake. I'll see to that, Ms. Korner. Thank you for pointing it out. It must have escaped my attention because I had the document yesterday before me, but must have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure we would all like to sit on Saturday to catch up on lost time, but ... Thank you. Your Honour, may I just very briefly deal with one matter? Your Honours may recall in the absence of Mr. Ackerman, I think it was a couple of weeks ago, I raised the question of the interview of Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the search had been done. And what I intended to do that day but never gave to you was a short summary of anything that could be remotely relevant. We don't consider it to be relevant. We're not proposing to disclose it. But under Rule 66(C), we're going to hand this in to Your Honours to see whether you would wish us to disclose anything to the Defence. It's the Milosevic speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so can I hand in one copy for each of Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We'll deal with that. And if it's the case of disclosure, we will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, it's two-sided copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Can we bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This concerns the starting of the Prijedor phase of this case. I don't remember the date. It's been a long time ago when I raised the question of when would either translation or tapes be available of all these transcripts that were given us with regard to Prijedor. I inquired about it again last week and was told that hopefully part of them could be put in my locker on Friday, and apparently the problem is that there are people who consider it necessary to listen to them very carefully and make sure that there's nothing contained in the tapes that they shouldn't disclose to us, and that's taking an enormous amount of time to do that. The thing I'm beginning to fear is this: That we have days and days and days and days, and I can't tell you how many days of transcripts of testimony that Mr. Brdjanin needs to have an opportunity to listen to. It could be helpful to me if Mr. Trbojevic would have an opportunity to listen to it, and it might be, Your Honour, that you will have to use your considerable influence to speed up the people that are supposedly trying to get this done, because we're getting to a very critical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can fix a time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- critical stage for delivery of those tapes. One thing you could do, like he just suggested, is you could say if they're not delivered by a certain date, the witness can't be called, or something like that. But it's just we're under enough stress regarding getting ready for Prijedor without having to also deal with this if there's a way to fix it. It may be a systemic problem that we have to wait for. I don't know. But I want to make inquiry now so that I can't be accused of having not done so. And I understand there is objective evidence this morning, today, as to how hard I've been working on all these matters, because I decided, instead of taking time to go to a barber and get my hair cut properly, I would try to do it myself, and I was just informed that I botched it pretty badly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is, basically, I have to say, this should be a Registry job, that they handed it over to the OTP because what we have to do is listen to the tapes in order to make sure that contained on it is not closed-session or private testimony of other witnesses on the same tape. There has been someone going through all the tapes, and we're going to check now as to what the situation is. But as I say, basically, I don't -- I think we're lumbered with it, but it's the usual thing. It's a question of finding the staff to do this. However, that's -- it's -- the only things I think that are still awaiting are the Stakic ones, obviously because they're very recent. The earlier transcripts, or tapes, are already with Mr. Ackerman, as I understand it. That's just the Stakic ones that he hasn't got.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case. I'm willing to reconsider my position on that, but I don't think I've gotten any of those tapes. But maybe I have. Maybe they were part of the large boxes of tapes that have been delivered earlier in the courtroom and were given to Mr. Brdjanin in the courtroom. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as Mr. Ackerman has given up signing receipts some time ago, I can't wave the receipts in front of Your Honour, but I'm assured that Mr. Ackerman was given a large number of tapes some time ago and we'll give the date if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the next one in line over here? Because Mr. Ackerman commented yesterday that it would take him about half an hour. Thank you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully you won't stay long today, but before we commence, may I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman will be resuming his cross-examination of you, and after that we see what the position will be. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've told us the last two days that you've been here about your opposition to Kljuc becoming part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I'm wondering: Do you recall ever signing any kind of a document in which you, in effect, recognised the existence and legitimacy of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall signing any document that had anything to do with the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have signed something during the initial talks, when it was said that it would be a region organised on economic relations, based on economic relations, and not any kind of autonomous Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But would it be your position that you didn't sign any kind of a document, like after May 7?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not after the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at Exhibit P905. That document contains your signature, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you deny that it's your signature?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall signing a whole series of documents on the 12th of May, 1992, many more than this particular one?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not even speak about the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. This is a statement about the wages in the area of Kljuc municipality, and it is possible that I did sign some documents, as I was the president of the -- the chairman of the executive board of the assembly. However, this document here, I don't think this is my signature. I don't think I ever signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document does actually speak of ARK in paragraph 1, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you have the same document that I'm looking at. Could the usher show me the document you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 905. Is it Exhibit 905?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the exhibit number that you mentioned, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are a number of documents attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He doesn't have the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are about three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document he should have is 0057532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's check. Madam Chuqing is going to check.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P905.3, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you have a copy -- is it both sides or do you have the English text? Pardon? Yes, but obviously he needs to see the one in the original language, and then you put it for some time on the ELMO too for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to just that first paragraph, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, may I ask the technicians to focus on the text that the witness is looking at at the moment, if that is possible, where his signature appears, in other words, if that is possible. I don't want whether technically that is possible or not. Alternatively, we'll put it on the ELMO, because I wanted it to be visible to everyone who is following these proceedings from outside the courtroom. Is it signed? Yes. And may I ask you to repeat the same question now, Mr. Ackerman, because obviously the question and the answer that we had before no longer -- they no longer make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you're now looking at a document that has an ERN number of 00575323, and I think it's Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- 905.3. And my question now is: Is that your signature that appears on that document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads clearly here: President of the executive board, typewritten, Asim Egrlic, and there's a signature, in pencil, and the signature belongs to Tihomir Dakic and not to Asim Egrlic. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is Tihomir Dakic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tihomir Dakic was the vice-president of the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he have authority to sign in your behalf?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the absence of the person who should have signed, he did have the authority to sign this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does have your name printed on there, doesn't it, Asim Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. It also has the appropriate stamp attached to it, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not exactly carry this stamp in my pocket, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. It also does not -- it also does refer, in paragraph 1, to ARK, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what the reference is here, but I see this document for the first time now, and I have never signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is very simple. It does refer to ARK in paragraph 1, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put the English version for a while? Okay. All right. You can remove the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman, and thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I can have my English version back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you now to be given a document, Exhibit DB96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the English version, usher? Please place it on the ELMO straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, what you should have before you is a statement made by a person by the name of Ismet Muratagic on 17 June of 1992. Is that what you have?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to refer to some of the things that Mr. Muratagic says in this statement and ask you if you agree that these things happened. He says about two months ago, which would have been mid-April of 1992, the people of the Krasulje village area demanded that military preparations and organisation begin and requested that guards be placed in villages and hamlets. Did that occur, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with what exactly they were looking for in Krasulje, but I do know that guards, village guards, were organised, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page? There's a paragraph that begins with the language: "On one occasion about a month and a half ago ..." Let me know when you've found that paragraph so you can follow me when I read it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. "On one occasion, about a month and a half ago, Mirzet Zukanovic said that I should go to a meeting in Pudin Han and that Omer Filipovic, MBO president, and Asim Egrlic, SDA president, would attend that meeting. I told him that I was not a member of any party and that I should not go to the meeting. He explained that it was not going to be a party meeting and that instructions for establishing armed formations in Muslim-populated villages would be given at the meeting. Omer Filipovic, Asim Egrlic, Muhamed Filipovic, Ibrahim Egrlic, Amir Avdic, Salih Salihovic, a man called Kedo and I were present at the meeting." Were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember attending this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about this meeting taking place around the first part of May?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only meetings of the executive board of the party were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you now go down and skip -- skip the next paragraph and go down to a paragraph that begins with the language: "Several days later ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Several days later, we held another meeting in Pudin Han, attended by Aziz Gromilic, Omer Filipovic, Asim Egrlic, Ibrahim Egrlic, Amir Avdic, Ferid Islamagic, Kedo, Fahrudin from Velagici, a man called Enes and me. We analysed the lists of men and weapons, on the basis of which Amir Avdic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. made an assessment as to how many days these forces could carry out combat operations using this MTS equipment and materiel. I remember that there were about 200 men on the list for Krasulje village, and we had the following weapons: Approximately 40 automatic rifles, 3 semi-automatic rifles, 50 pistols, 50 hunting rifles, 3 sniper rifles, 1 7.62 millimetre PM light machine-gun, 1 M-53 PM, 30 hand grenades and 4 Zolja hand-held rockets. There was about 12.000 rounds of ammunition and various calibres. At that meeting I was appointed company commander in Krasulje." Do you recall that meeting and were you present?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this meeting was ever held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Ismet Muratagic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole town knows him, because he was a maintenance worker for electrical appliances and he had a shop in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go on then to maybe the next page, there's a paragraph that begins: "At the end of the meeting ..." It says: "At the end of the meeting, Omer Filipovic distributed cards." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Omer Filipovic distributed cards among us, with BH TO written on them and first and last names were to be written on the back of those cards. We were to give the cards only to those who agreed to join the new TO." Do you know anything about those cards that Omer Filipovic was distributing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to see these cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about the cards being printed, but I've never seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you go down now to the next paragraph that begins with: "The day after the meeting, Aziz Gromilic ..." And go down that paragraph to where he says: "I agreed and took my company below Bajrami village. I deployed the men and ordered that positions be fortified, that is, that dugouts be made." Do you know whether any positions were actually established at that location and that dugouts were made there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not aware of that. What I do know is that there were village guards there, but that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'll go now probably to the next page, there's a paragraph after there's a whole series of names. Then there's a paragraph begins with: "After we were deployed at the position ..." And it has the name Aziz Gromilic in it. I think it's actually the next paragraph after the one we just looked at. It begins with: "After we were deployed at the position, Aziz Gromilic ..."

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "After we were deployed at the position, Aziz Gromilic put up a wooden barricade on the road at the approach to Krasulje village, although nobody had ordered him to do that." Do you know if there actually was a wooden barricade put up on that road approaching Krasulje village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to skip the next paragraph, and then the following one begins with: "I returned to the position ..." Let me know when you've found that. Do you see it: "I returned to the position ..."?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this on page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be just one paragraph after the one we were just looking at about wooden barricades. There's a paragraph and then it's the one -- next one. It says: "I returned to the position in Bajrami village, and at about 1000 hours ..."

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "... an official police car came by, followed by a white van, and they stopped in front of the barricade. As they were pulling up and getting out of the cars, fire was opened on them from the position without anybody's order. I did not open fire immediately, but a couple of minutes later I fired five or six bullets in the direction of the policemen who held a position by the road." And then I'm skipping a little bit: "I could see the motionless body of a policeman lying by the road several metres behind the police car, and the others were nowhere to be seen, as they had fled to the nearby woods." Now, you do know that this happened, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that Omer Filipovic and Vinko Kondic actually arrived together at that scene?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this only once I arrived at the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you, Mr. Ackerman, because your question to the witness: You know that this happened? covers a whole multitude of events here. I suppose you wanted to question -- direct a question as to the event of the killing of the policeman only, and not as to the fact that the person making a statement fired five or six bullets, that a van came with the police, and the rest, because otherwise I would ask you to question the witness as to each and every part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour. I was referring to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, to the killing, to the incident and not the manner in which it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm finished with this document. You may return it now. And I'd like you to be given P854. The document I've handed you, sir, refers - and I think it's perhaps a Kljuc Radio document - refers to a meeting held in Kljuc on the 25th of June of what probably has to be the year 1991, and it is -- refers to a meeting, a public discussion in the big hall of the Kljuc community centre, and the guest was Professor Muhamed Filipovic. My question is: Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I won't ask you any questions -- did you hear about it? Did you hear about what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this for the first time, so I'm unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm being told something, and I don't understand what I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I'm told that my question to you was translated -- let me just ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The meeting was held, as I understand it, on 25 June 1991, not 1992? Does that change your view about whether you attended the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you hear the report on the radio about this meeting? Do you know about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished, then, with that document. Yesterday in your testimony you were asked by Ms. Korner about the 6th Krajina Brigade, and you told us that you believed the 6th Krajina Brigade was present in Kljuc on or about the 7th of May. And you were then asked how you knew it was the 6th Krajina Brigade, and you said it was because they had come from the direction of Kljuc. Correct? I'm sorry. Direction of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there anything else which lets you conclude that they were the 6th Krajina Brigade, other than the direction from which they had come?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some men contacted the men who had become as reservists to the territory of Kljuc municipality, and they told them they were from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just made the conclusion on the basis of the fact that they had come from the direction of Sanski Most, where that brigade was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now, sir, to Manjaca, after you were taken to Manjaca, and you talked to us yesterday about the death and Omer Filipovic, and you said that he was returned to the stables and that you were in the same stable, or were you in the same stable that he was in the day before he died?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the neighbouring stable, but movement was allowed, and I was able to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how it was he left that stable that night?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I didn't see him -- that he went out and that he went towards the wire. Between the wire fence, there was a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he was called out?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the guards pulled him out of some sort of a trench that was nearby, be it near the fence, near the barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't hear him being called out of the stable, though, did you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the same stable, so I can't say. I just saw when they released him from the isolation cell, that he entered the stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know about what time it was you heard these incidents going on outside? Just your best guess, best estimate.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him coming from the isolation cell, that was in the afternoon, and then, after a certain period of time, towards evening, they sent him back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said -- do you know how it was -- I asked you: "Do you know how it was he left the stable that night?" And you said: "I heard that." Did you hear that from someone or did you actually hear things going on outside?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from other detainees that they heard shouts of the guards calling him out by name to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You didn't hear those shouts yourself, though?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday during your testimony you told us about your wife leaving Kljuc and how she had to sign a statement turning over all the property to Republika Srpska. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you -- I think you indicated that anyone leaving had to sign a similar statement as the one your wife signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please look at P1119 again, please. This is the statement you were talking about that people were required to sign before they left Kljuc municipality, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please show us where in this statement it says that she turns property over to Republika Srpska. Let me know when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the heading, it says: "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kljuc municipality, commission for gathering information on resettlement of the population from Kljuc municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. I didn't ask you what the heading said. I asked you: Where in the document does it say that she is turning her property over to Republika Srpska? Find that part and tell me where it is.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, according to the heading itself, you can see that it is Republika Srpska, which is above Kljuc municipality, and that the property is being handed over to Kljuc municipality, and therefore also to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me where it says -- tell me where it says in the document that the property is being handed over to Kljuc municipality or Republika Srpska. It doesn't say that in the heading, sir.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the heading, it says that it is the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kljuc municipality, and then it says record. What is being handed over. There is the signature of my wife and the names of the people who took the statement down. It says here who the president of the commission is, and everything else. I don't see anything disputed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me where it says: Here is the property that I'm handing over to Republika Srpska. Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that literally, but it's sufficient that we see that it says up there "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kljuc municipality." Then it is quite clear to everyone that this document, referring to this, means that it's being turned over to Kljuc municipality, that is, to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your position that under the law of Yugoslavia that existed at that time, that the Kljuc municipality could use this document to prove that they owned the property listed in that document, that this is a legal transfer of property? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who made this up and forced people to sign such documents when leaving the territory of the municipality could answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the one you can answer is what you made up, and what you made up was that this document transfers property of Republika Srpska, and it doesn't in any way, does it? That's just a myth of yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used it in that way because they had allotted my house, and others, to people who had stayed behind, which means Serbs. So Bosniak houses were given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your house was among those houses that was allotted to Serbs, then, was it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when was it your house was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was destroyed at the beginning, but it wasn't just the house. The house stands on land and there's land around the house, and the foundations and the walls and what was left of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they allotted it to a Serb. Who was the Serb? Was it a refugee?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't investigate. In any case, they had allotted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then it's your position that almost immediately they kicked that Serb out and destroyed it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's obviously a mix-up in the order of things. First of all, people were forced out of their houses and resettled upon signing such documents and obliging them to pay all the dues they owed, and then the houses were looted. Some were torched. And after a certain period of time, they would allot houses, after some time had elapsed, and when people did not come back after a certain period of time - it may have been a year or two - they started allotting and distributing these houses, because they reckoned the Bosniaks would never come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know. You weren't there when your house was destroyed, were you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that your house was destroyed much later, when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina re-took Kljuc? Could it have been destroyed at that time, in the fighting involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't destroyed then, because my wife told me how this had happened, that the house was set on fire, that she watched this from another village where she was staying in her father's house. So that it is known full well when the house was set on fire. And when I returned to Kljuc, I found just rubble. So there's nothing questionable. I don't know whether I have made myself clear enough. I think everything is quite clear. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that people were forced out of their houses and forced to sign documents like you showed us the one your wife signed, and they were obliged to pay all the dues that they owed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "the dues they owed," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is, for instance, if one had to pay one's telephone bill by mid-month, they would have to pay it. If he was leaving in the middle of the month, he would have to pay his electricity bill for that half month, his taxes, and to sign this document turning over all their immobile property to this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that if you wanted to leave Kljuc today and move to a different municipality, that you would have to pay all those things before you left?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. If I'm leaving temporarily. But if somebody is being expelled permanently, this was a sign that they required that all dues be paid because they thought these people would never come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't mean to ask you temporarily. I meant to ask you permanently. If you were permanently going to leave the Kljuc municipality today, you're required to make all those payments, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be normal to do so, if one is moving away, under normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what your wife said in the statement that she gave them was that she was "leaving the Kljuc municipality with my family for good, of my own free will." Right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife was not consulted as to what she would write down. What she was given, she signed, just to save her life and that of her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Re-examination, Ms. Korner. Ms. Korner has got some further questions to you, and then we come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, yesterday it was put to you by Mr. Ackerman - Your Honour, at page 35, LiveNote, page 35 - "Do you know that a coordinator is simply a person who coordinates bodies and has no authority in their own right? Do you know that?" And you said: "Yes, I do." That was in reference to the telex that you intercepted. Do you remember that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what power Mr. Brdjanin had at the time that he sent that telex?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was vice-president of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what, in your experience, what sort of power or what sort of position did that give him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, the vice-president of the Assembly has the same authority as the president, and if he is entrusted with the authority of a coordinator, that would mean also executive authority in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So when you -- on the face of your answer yesterday, you agreed with the proposition that was put to you by Mr. Ackerman, that a coordinator has no authority in their own right. Can you explain on what basis you were agreeing with Mr. Ackerman, in the light of your present answer?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was put to me in general terms: What kind of authority a coordinator has. And the word itself says that he coordinates something. However, in this case, it was not just any coordinator but the vice-president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to another matter that you were asked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, at page 38 and 39 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were being asked about the document, the communique that was put out in June of 1991. And just to remind ourselves of the exhibit number which I think ... Yes. Exhibit P853, please. This was the statement that was put out by yourself and Mr. Filipovic, and you were asked about an answer that you had given, in which you said that attempts were being made to get Kljuc to join the Bosanska Krajina region, and it was put to you that you had made that answer up because the Autonomous Region of Krajina had not yet come into existence in June of 1991. Had you heard of the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina region in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about this community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want you to have a look, please, at the document P3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you've got the volume 1 of the Kljuc binders, it's two before 853, one of the early documents. It's also got two numbers, 851 and 853. And I think we had better have the -- for a moment, could we have the B/C/S put onto the ELMO, and we'll look at the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so that we can all see -- no, usher. I want the top bit. Thank you. Stop. The date there, the 10th of April, 1991, and if you could give that to the witness now. We can take it off the ELMO and put the English translation on the ELMO, because the date was missed out of the English translation. And there we see that in April a decision, signed by the municipal president, Jovo Banjac, states that the previously adopted decision regarding the Kljuc municipality joining the Banja Luka community of municipalities is hereby confirmed, affirming the fact that the municipality of Kljuc is part of the regional community of Bosanska Krajina, now the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. So it appears that this was referring back to a decision in April of 1991. Is that correct, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you issued that communique in June of 1991, were you aware of this decision and the earlier one, rather, the decision of the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wrote about this. There is a public announcement about this. The first decision was passed without the Assembly convening, and then we immediately issued a public statement. And due to the pressure we received from the public, we put this proposal forward at the Assembly. So this subject was discussed on a number of occasions and certain conclusions were reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you, on behalf of the SDA, content to see Kljuc becoming part of the Banja Luka community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Banja Luka community of municipalities is concerned, Kljuc used indeed to be part of that community, and it was a regional organisation based on economic relations. As soon as this idea about the Autonomous Region came up, we could not accept it, because what it meant was an autonomous entity within the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would have meant that, as had earlier been proclaimed, this entity would be made to join Serbia, which would in no way be beneficial to the Bosniaks and Muslims in the area, and that was the reason why we refused it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we turn to another topic along the same lines? You were shown the constitution of the -- and the Statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Did you ever see that published before you were shown it by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the part that was read to you, you were shown the part which, on the face of it, guaranteed or stated: "All nations and nationalities in the Autonomous Region shall be equal in their rights and duties, without distinction as to race, sex, birth," et cetera. Now, at the time, if you had seen that, would you have accepted that the Autonomous Region of Krajina would guarantee the rights of all nationalities, regardless of sex, birth, language, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even in that case. We would not have accepted that, because the Autonomous Region was organised without regard for the constitution of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we, the Bosniaks, as a different ethnic group, held a referendum, an independence referendum for independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was held on the 28th of February and the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What nationality, or what nationalities, formed the government of the Autonomous Region? Was it ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next I want to ask you about -- yes. You were asked about the document P167, which was the order signed by Lieutenant Colonel Sajic, as to the surrender of weapons by the 11th of May. And it was put to you that it applied to all persons illegally in possession of weapons. Against whom was that order of disarmament enforced?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard on the radio, it only applied to the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it apply only to illegally held weapons, in other words, weapons held without a permit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Only weapons without permit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When weapons were seized or handed over, were weapons seized which were lawfully owned, did have a permit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those weapons were seized too, even hunting weapons were seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown today a document that Exhibit P905 has your typewritten signature on it that you say that the signature is that of Mr. Tihomir Dakic, I think. Before you were shown that document today, had you ever seen that before?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, were you still signing documents that related to the executive committee of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, all Bosniaks were expelled from Kljuc municipality, and no one signed anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally this, Mr. Egrlic: You were shown a statement signed by a Mr. -- it's DB96. I've forgotten what the gentleman's name is now. And you said you knew him because he was a maintenance man in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have a copy? Perhaps you had better have it back again, DB96.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Muratagic. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was detained at the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This appears to have been taken by the CSB in Banja Luka, this particular statement, though it's dated the same day as the record of interview with you. Do you know the circumstances under which he made this statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gentleman had been taken for interviews many times, and I know that he would always return in a very bad state, because he had been beaten every single time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that's all I ask in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask one question about Exhibit P3, which Ms. Korner brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I hear the question first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would like the witness to look at the question and just confirm from the contents of that document that it is a typographical error and the date is 1992, not 1991. And that's certainly the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will allow that question. Just show the witness that and ask him to confirm that the date is 1992 and not 1991

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to ask you to read the contents of that document, and isn't it the case from what is contained within that document that it's clear that the date on it is a typographical error and it should be 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, before we go -- can we stop, please, Your Honour, before this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was dealt with by Dr. Donja. That's why -- if we go back and look at it, there was a decision taken in 1991 -- that's why he dealt with it, because he was dealing with the progression of the Bosnian community municipalities into that. They took a decision, or attempted to take a decision in 1991, to join, but it never worked. And it's referring back to that, Your Honour, if we look up the testimony of Dr. Donja. So it's not a mis -- a typing. Of course it refers -- this decision is undated and it refers to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. But in actual fact, it's referring back to 1991, and that's why it's such an early document. So I think before -- unless he's going to say that the date is wrongly typed, but certainly -- this is not the date of the document, I agree, the 10th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the translation is clearly not correct, because it does not contain what appears on the first line of the B/C/S. The first line of the B/C/S has 10/4/1991 in it. That doesn't appear in the translation. So the translation is totally -- it's certainly incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the reason why Ms. Korner first asked for the B/C/S version to be put on the ELMO, making it clear that the English version did not contain the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm having a little sense of deja vu, Your Honour. I think we went through this with this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- when Dr. Donja testified, and the Prosecution was going to substitute a proper translation. And I don't know that that's been done, but it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we obviously have here does not reflect -- yes. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Ackerman no longer wants the witness to go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not. I now remember more about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Usher, please take the document back from the witness. He need not answer that question. So, thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Egrlic, that brings us to the end of your testimony in this trial, before this Tribunal, before this Court, Trial Chamber. You will be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher and taken care of, pending your return to your country. On behalf of the -- all the members of this Tribunal, I would like to take this opportunity to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence. You will now be escorted. Thank you, and have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the next witness does not have any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he doesn't, Your Honour. Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm either fiddling with the microphone or I don't put it on. Mr. Nicholls will call the witness and there's no protective measures. The majority of the tapes of the Prijedor witnesses were disclosed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the Defence on the 21st of February and the 1st of March of this year. All that are outstanding to -- at the moment are some of the -- are the Stakic tapes, and we're trying to get them copied now, but the other ones have all been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's appropriate to say that since then probably a lot of water has passed under the bridges and I hope they have not washed away --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the only thing before Mr. Ackerman leaps to his feet to complain is to check his own. Even if he won't sign the receipts, he must keep a record of what he gets somewhere. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come back to us on this, Mr. Ackerman. Please confirm that this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite certain it's correct. I remember them giving me large boxes of tapes which were immediately handed over to the guards to take to the Detention Centre for Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic to listen to, and I think they have done that and I'm satisfied that we have everything bit the Stakic tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless I learn differently. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to need --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have to get the Stakic Rule 98 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That has to be done by the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know when the first break was planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first break will be in ten minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I wonder if anybody agrees to take that now. I can use the time to set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can take the break now if you want and call the witness immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that make sense rather than get through his name and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We will have -- shall we all try to finish as on previous occasions by 6.30 rather than 7.00? So that means shortening the breaks, obviously. All right? So 15 minutes, 20 minutes. Twenty minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ticevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that very soon you will be giving evidence. You will start giving evidence in a couple of minutes' time. And it is the rule of this Tribunal that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration, which, for all intents and purposes of law is equivalent to an oath, where that is applicable, the text is contained in a piece of paper that the usher is going to give to you, and my request to you is to make that solemn declaration by reading the text, and that will be your commitment with this Court to tell us the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a piece of paper which I believe has Christmas and New Year dates on it correctly. I will hand it to Chuqing Chen and then I will ask your permission to be excused for the balance of the afternoon to work on Prijedor matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Ackerman. Who will be taking over? Mr. Trbojevic, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can either remain seated where you are or change places with Mr. Ackerman, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ticevic, again, now that you're sitting down, let me explain to you exactly where you are and what's going to happen. You are a witness in a trial that has been going on for some time, on an indictment presented against the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin. The procedure here is a very simple one, and it's more or less identical to that in most other criminal courts, or courts of criminal jurisdiction. Basically, it will first be the Prosecution that will put to you a number of questions, and your duty is to answer those questions as truthfully as possible and as accurately as possible and as fully as possible, unless we, the three Judges, direct you not to answer a particular question or stop you from continuing with your answer. After that, it will be the Defence team that will cross-examine you, in other words, the lawyers for the accused have got the right to put questions to you too. That is a fundamental right that the accused has, and you have no right to distinguish between the Prosecution and the Defence. Your duty is to answer questions truthfully and fully and accurately, irrespective of who is putting them to you. Again, we will protect you if you are harassed. We will stop any questions that we may consider not appropriate and you will be asked not to answer any questions that we feel shouldn't be answered by you. Having premised that, I'll just introduce the Chamber. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Agius and I come from Malta. To my right I am flanked Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and to my left by Judge Taya from Japan. Mr. Nicholls is the Officer of the Prosecution that will conduct the examination-in-chief. I suppose you have already met and therefore you're familiar with his face. And then later on I will advise you as to who will be cross-examining you, whether it's Mr. Ackerman, the lead counsel for the Defence, or his co-counsel, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Nicholls, the witness is all yours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may [Previous translation continues] ... while you're answering questions and the interpreters will let you know if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to first move through some background information and try to do that quite quickly, and then go right into the events of late 1991 and into 1992 in Kljuc. Sir, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Nisvet Ticevic. I was born on the 24th of June, 1966, in Pudin Han, Kljuc municipality, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you are a Bosniak and --

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- and you practice the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you went to -- you say you grew up in Kljuc, and after beginning high school, you then moved to Switzerland to work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you return to Kljuc from Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: In late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do when you returned to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you could just briefly describe Kljuc municipality. What was the majority ethnic group in that - sorry - in Pudin Han? Was that a Muslim village or a Serb village, or what type of a village was that?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Pudin Han was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you first returned in late 1991, had you noticed whether relations between the different ethnic groups in Kljuc municipality had changed at all?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how were they different when you had left after high school and gone to Switzerland? What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many differences. People started losing faith in one another. There was curfew. At that time, the Republika Srpska was about to be proclaimed, so there was a lot of tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there were any problems or disruptive behaviour in Pudin Han while you were a waiter there in late 1991? Was anybody causing any problems at night?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Reservists and the JNA returning from the front in Croatia, they would shoot at houses, at villages facilities. They would maltreat people, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were they maltreating all people or predominantly the Muslim population in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They maltreated the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during this time, were there any military convoys passing through the area of your village?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: As my municipality and my village are -- straddled the so-called Avnoj road, there were convoys passing through on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What type of convoys were these?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Military convoys, sometimes large convoys, sometimes smaller ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did these convoys cause any problems as they passed through or did they pass through peacefully?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Those convoys were causing problems. As I said, they maltreated the population. They shot at houses and religious facilities. They raised three fingers up in the air, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you talked about "they." Do you mean to say there was firing from these convoys at houses and at religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question was: Was the -- just to be very clear: Was the firing that you talked about at houses and at religious buildings, I presume you mean mosques, was that firing coming from the convoys passing through?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely from lorries with soldiers and weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you had mentioned a curfew. Do you remember when that curfew began -- was imposed, was first imposed?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was after the autonomous republic of Serbian Krajina was proclaimed. Curfew was introduced, but only for non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who -- what body introduced that curfew, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic, Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in late -- well, at any time late 1991 into 1992, were there any checkpoints or roadblocks set up in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, military checkpoints had been set up in Velagici, in Pudin Han, in all the more prominent locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you know, which units were in charge of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I do. There was the police, the Serbian police manning the checkpoints, the reservists, and some Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in response to all these problems which you've talked about, the shooting at the houses and religious buildings, the drunken behaviour, did the Muslim population find -- attempt to deal with those problems? Was there any solution which you and other men in your community pursued in order to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, led by our legally elected president, Omer Filipovic and Asim Egrlic, we tried to keep war from happening. However, we couldn't reach a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. In your statement you talked about night patrols being formed. Can you tell us what the night patrols were?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Night patrols were simply for our own safety, the safety of our families, and for our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when were these night patrols first formed?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer this question with any precision. Some people had already begun with that, but after Republika Srpska had been proclaimed, it was in a more massive scale throughout the villages. We began setting up guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you personally took part in night patrols in Pudin Han; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us: How -- when you took part in a night patrol, how was that patrol set up? How was it decided who would take part in it and what parts of the village would be guarded?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There were no decisions made. It was more a thing among neighbours. You would have several young men from each of the villages, and they would spend a night just guarding the village. There were no specific decisions being made as to who should go where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was participation in these night patrols voluntary or was it mandatory? Could somebody be ordered to take part in a night patrol?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no one could order it to anyone. Each one did as he thought best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what -- well, what type of weapons did the men you knew carry when they were on night patrol when they were guarding their villages?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It was mostly pistols or hunting rifles. Those who were well off, they purchased weapons themselves. There was no weapons -- there were no weapons being distributed. It was up to each individual to find one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while on patrol, would these patrols be confined to the village and to defend the village or would they be in any way offensive patrols, in other words, going to other villages or initiating any type of combat?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Those patrols were there just to protect our village and our lives, but not to go to other villages or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there any -- you've pretty much answered this, but was there any kind of commander for the night patrols which you were on? Was there any kind of boss for your night patrol group?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during this time, you knew Omer Filipovic quite well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was your relationship to him? How did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I've known Omer for a long time. He was a teacher in Kljuc, and also as a neighbour. I didn't have any particular contact with him before the war. I didn't socialise with him, but I knew him as a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in late 1991/1992, in your statement you refer to yourself as his courier. Explain what exactly that means.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can. This wasn't in 1991. It was the moment when the shooting started in my village. As the people were in panic, in fear, he did designate certain people who would, in a sense, advise the people to stay in one place so as not to go to the woods in groups, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And according to your statement, you attended in 1992 some meetings with Omer Filipovic. If you can tell me, just broadly, in your own words: What was his goal at this time? What was he trying to achieve in relation to the problems that the Muslims and the Serbs were having together?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that Omer Filipovic was the legally elected president of our people in the legally recognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was our legal representative in Kljuc municipality. And as the people who had given him our trust, we believed in him. Omer Filipovic was never in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. favour of war. He was for peace. And never for a moment did he say to anyone that he was preparing for war, or anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd like to now -- well, do you remember going into early May, a time when the police changed their uniforms and began changing the insignia which they wore on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was a loyalty oath required of all policemen at that time?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: All non-Serb policemen were required to express their loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P171, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you'd just take a look at that document, please.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just the first three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As far as you remember, the date on this document is the 7th of May, 1992. It's a public announcement from the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc municipality and it describes the change in the uniforms and that the municipal building will now be displaying a Serbian flag as the municipality of Kljuc is now a part of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Does that all fit with what you remember happening during that week in May?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but what doesn't fit is that the livelihood of those workers who do not sign the solemn oath would not be threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened to the --

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't be in jeopardy, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened to workers who refused to sign that solemn loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They were mistreated, taken to camp, some were even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can move on now a few weeks to the 27th of May, 1992, and what happened in Pudin Han on that day, in the Pudin Han area.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait one second. And I'm going to specifically ask you questions about the incident of firing between a convoy that was passing through the area of Pudin Han and some Muslim men in that area. Now, were you present when that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe, simply for the Court, please: Before the convoy came through the area, what were you doing? What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Before the convoy passed, I wasn't there. Once the shooting started -- the shooting was provoked by the Serb police going to the village of Krasulje and seizing weapons from non-Serbs. So the people of Krasulje would not allow them to seize their weapons. There was an exchange of fire, in which a Serb policeman, known as Dule was killed. Some were wounded, some fled. So that when this happened, the people in Pudin Han had heard of what had happened, and then we started to prepare for defence, because we knew we would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. How did you prepare for that defence? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Simply, the people started to panic. So we got together to see what we should do if they should launch an attack on our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do to prepare for an attack you thought might be coming?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: First, the local people, the villagers who were closest to the town of Kljuc, those who lived closest to Kljuc, they formed a kind of line in the event of the Serb army attacking, and they wanted to put up resistance to protect their families. But because our citizens were provoked on a daily basis by the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska, our people lost their nerve, and that day when the convoy came, opening fire on our religious buildings and our homes, individuals simply provoked that incident, opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go through it step by step. This convoy, how many vehicles were in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There may have been two or three buses and two trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At what time -- well, you actually saw this convoy coming through on the 27th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where exactly did you first see the convoy on the 27th? Where was that in relation to Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I saw them in the village of Draganovici, and that is a place close to where the shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe we should give you a map to help us.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is going to be Exhibit P1111?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you give me the next number in the sequence that we have been following? I think 1120.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 1120, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at the map to your left.
