utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you see the road which runs from Kljuc through Hadzici towards Velagici?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that the road where this incident with the convoy took place?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just, please, mark that road with an "X" as close as you can to where this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least on my monitor, the image is quite out of focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's not for me, because I have the map in any case, and I know what's happening, but for the public ... I think you can zoom on the area that we're talking about. Zoom on Kljuc, Hadzici, and Velagici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I know that because of the scale of this map, that's an approximation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But can I ask you also to put your initials, please, next to that mark that you put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there a problem? Is there a problem? Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the convoy, before the shooting started, was it -- it was heading towards Kljuc, is that right, on that road?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as this convoy came towards Kljuc, through the road, what was happening, just to be very clear, which caused the Muslim men to shoot at the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago that there was provocation, mistreatment, shooting, opening fire at houses and religious buildings, and that was what happened that day too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is specifically: When this convoy of soldiers came through towards Kljuc, was there any shooting from the convoy? Was there anybody on the trucks or buses shooting at houses, shooting at anybody, or was that convoy coming through peacefully, on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: That convoy was not passing peacefully. We were in Hadzici. The distance between Hadzici and Pudin Han is one kilometre, so that we knew that the shooting that happened in Pudin Han was done by the same people who had opened fire at Hadzici, so that our boys returned fire. There were two civilian trucks going by with materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you say "our boys," how many men -- what do you mean by that? How many men were there who you're referring to as "our boys"?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There were 300 to 400, but they were not all shooting. There were women and children and men who came out to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where were you in relation to the road? Could you actually see any of this shooting or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I saw the shooting. I was maybe 30 or 50 metres away, on the right-hand side of the convoy, when it's heading towards Kljuc, in a wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do when you heard the shooting start?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything just then, but many guys who were shooting, I don't myself know how to put it. This was the first time for me to experience anything like this. And then a few minutes later I went off to see Omer Filipovic in the centre to let him know what was happening, because I was a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we get to that, could you tell whether there were any casualties amongst the people in the convoy? Was anybody injured or killed, that you could tell, at that time?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a driver of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how could you tell that? Describe what you saw, if you can, before we go to what you did next.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can describe it. Some men before me, or many of us, had already gone to that truck. As far as I know, the driver was in the truck. But those who had gone there before had dragged him out of the truck, and he was lying down next to the fence, next to the road. He was lying there dead, killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were starting to say that after this you went to report what had happened to Omer Filipovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was his reaction when you told him what had happened?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: He was very angry, and he called some men to go and see what was going on, people he trusted, to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why was he angry? At the way it had occurred or that somebody had been killed or that there is any shooting at all? If you can just describe why he was angry it as best you can.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omer Filipovic, until the last moment - and I was next to him - was in favour of peace, and he would never allow any one of us to be provoked to enter into a conflict. Because we had -- we stood no chance against such a force. However, some men did what they did, people he could not give orders to, so I know right up until he was captured that he was in favour of peace, and he was killed, and still he favoured peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did anybody order an attack on that convoy, order that an ambush be set up to shoot at that convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: On our side, no one could give orders to anyone. I state that with full responsibility. But I'm saying that there were individuals who were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Omer's reaction? There was a meeting, was there not, to discuss the situation after you told Omer Filipovic about what had happened with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Omer's reaction was that he sent me to the surrounding villages and hamlets, Zavidovici and Krasulje, to see the reaction of the people. And as Omer had friends among the Serbs, a person called Kondic, the chief of police in Kljuc, who was a Serb, he hoped that things would settle down and peace would be restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're referring to Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you attend any meeting, or were you at any meeting with Omer Filipovic and Vinko Kondic about this situation after the incident in Krasulje which you've told us about where the policeman was killed and after this shooting with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. The first meeting occurred in the village of Krasulje, that is, Omer guaranteed to Vinko Kondic that he could come and he would be safe in Krasulje, to take away the dead policeman, Duca. And that was their first agreement and meeting. A second meeting was in Pudin Han, that is, at a crossroads leading in three different directions: One towards Sanski Most, another towards Bosanska Petrovac, and a third to Kljuc. And they met there and discussed peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, was there any ultimatum or -- given at that time by Vinko Kondic that weapons be surrendered by the Muslims of Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic and Vinko Kondic were friends, and I personally heard Vinko say that the people should hand in their weapons and nothing would happen to them. And Omer believed him, as a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did -- was any deadline for the handover of weapons given, if you remember? Was any deadline set, I should say?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: A deadline was set. When Vinko Kondic left our territories and Omer returned to the youth centre in Pudin Han, and then an ultimatum was issued for the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember what day and what time those weapons were to be surrendered by?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think it was until 1700 hours the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P921.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you'll just take a moment to read the top portion of that document. That is an order of the Kljuc municipality Crisis Staff, and the order, it states, was issued at the meeting held on the 28th of May, 1992, at 8.00 a.m., in the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc municipality. Under item 1, the order states: "Calling all citizens who own illegally acquired weapons to hand them over today between the hours of noon and 1400 at the Kljuc Public Security Station, the Kljuc Territorial Defence headquarters, or the nearest police station. Otherwise, vigorous measures will be implemented to carry out disarmament, which could have disastrous consequences for the security of both people and property." Is that what it states in the version you're reading, the original, in your language?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Having read that, is that about the same deadline as what you were told, keeping in mind that this is now the next day, the 28th of May?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was up until 1700 hours, because Omer spoke to them on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Spoke to who?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but with representatives of the Serb authorities in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After this meeting on the 27th of May, you started to talk about returning to the youth centre. Can you tell us about the meeting at the youth centre in Pudin Han, where Omer Filipovic and the other citizens discussed whether or not to surrender their weapons as demanded by Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you about it. When we got back to the youth centre, Omer told the people there about the situation and about Vinko Kondic's conditions and the conditions imposed by Republika Srpska authorities in Kljuc. Eighty per cent of the people there realised that we stood no chance fighting a force that was stronger than us, and 20 per cent of the people refused to negotiate or surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many people were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. The whole village practically. Pudin Han, Hadzici, Donji Hadzici, Gornji Hadzici, Gornji Mojici, Donji Mojici, Velagici, and a number of other hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Omer Filipovic's recommendation? That the weapons Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. should be surrendered or not?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic was in favour of surrendering the weapons. He was a more experienced person than many of us there, so he realised that we stood no chance against a force as mighty as the force we were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But ultimately, was a decision made collectively to surrender the weapons, or not?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, 80 per cent of the population were in favour of surrendering, and 20 per cent were against surrendering weapons, and they left towards Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It was not only one meeting; it was a series of meetings, and there were many people attending. It was outside the youth centre, and the youth centre could not hold all those people. Omer was standing on a second-floor -- at a second-floor window and he was speaking to the people assembled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when -- what decision did you personally make at this meeting? Were you going to surrender your weapon or not?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I decided not to surrender my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what type of weapon or weapons did you personally have at this time?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I had a rifle. We call it Tandzara. And later I obtained a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And later on in your statement you talked about the shelling of Pudin Han which began after this meeting. Can you tell us about, if you remember, when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I remember, and I wish to say that, as we see in this document here, we were given an ultimatum of only two hours for several thousands of people. It's impossible to do that within only several hours for the whole population to surrender their weapons. So that means they were basically looking for an excuse to attack. The shelling began between 1800 hours and 2000 hours, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were you when the shelling of Pudin Han began?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was outside the youth centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can tell, where were those shells coming from? Where was -- which villages were the positions from which Pudin Han was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Small-calibre shells were falling from the direction of a hamlet to the right side of the road, if you head from Kljuc towards Pudin Han. The village is called Briscica heavy projectiles were coming from the direction of Laniste and Kopljanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did this shelling continue?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say precisely, because I was shocked too. It was the first time we experienced anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your statement, you talked about where the first shell landed and what happened when that shell landed. Do you remember now about the first shell landing outside the youth centre?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that first shell very well. The first shell that landed killed one of our men, Refik Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as these shells started landing, what did the people, the civilians and all the other people in Pudin Han do?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Amid the confusion, the people of Pudin Han started running towards Hripavac, the village of Balijevici. The shell hit the tractor full of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at this time that the shelling started, you talked about how there was a meeting and some people had decided to surrender their weapons and others -- and you among them refused to do so. How many armed men do you think there were in Pudin Han at the time the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Quite many people from where I lived purchased weapons, but when the shooting started, the 20 per cent of those who had refused to surrender their weapons started using their weapons, and the rest had just discarded their weapons out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is: If you know, if you remember, though, total, about how many men were there, people who had refused to surrender who were armed? I'm just trying to get -- if you can tell us how big a resistance there was in that village at that time.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I think there may have been between 400 and 500 pieces, firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then the same amount of men; is that what you're saying, 400 or 500 men who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to say that that was the approximate number of pieces, but I'm not sure that each of those individuals carried weapons at the time the shooting began.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you started telling us about a tractor that was hit by a shell. Do you know the names of the people who were killed in that shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I know some of the names, because I helped to bury those bodies personally. There was Refik Draganovic, born roughly in 1960. His wife; one of his sons, Hamdo Becic was there, born in 1966; his sister Esma; his wife was there too, born in the same year; and there was another lady from Reizovici. I don't know her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were these people part of any kind of armed resistance or were they trying to leave on that tractor?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians who tried to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe at that time, not at any time when you returned, but at that time, as a witness, to what you personally saw, not what you heard about or what you came back and saw later, what did the village look like? What was the effect of this shelling? Just so that you can give the Chamber an idea of the scale of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe the effects of the shelling in the village that you saw at the time of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: The effects were considerable. There were houses ablaze, cars too. The cattle and all the animals were killed. Many people got killed. I'm speaking about the day of our withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, tell me what you did once the shelling started and how you left and went into the woods with some other men.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: When we were sure that there were no civilians left in Pudin Han, the few of us who stayed behind withdrew in the direction of the village of Belijevic or Hripavci in the late hours of the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Omer Filipovic stay behind until about -- until everybody -- until you were sure all the civilians had left?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic stayed there, and that's also where he was captured, because he refused to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the time you left, were any soldiers coming into the village, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. When we were withdrawing, outside a restaurant we noticed their army coming out of a TAM truck, a TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which army was this?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It was the Republika Srpska army reservists, police force, and Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you told us in your -- you stated in your -- in the statement you gave to the OTP that you were pursued into the forest. Can you describe that, where you went in the forest and how you were pursued?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can describe this to you. The forest, which is perhaps a kilometre from the youth centre, there were many other civilians there, and we were stationed there until we could try to reach the village of Hripavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened there? Were you able to get to Hripavci or did you stay in the forest?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the forest that evening, and then when the rest of the civilians had withdrawn, we reached Hripavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your goal was to go to Bihac at that time?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And why was that? Just to be clear, why were you trying to get to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Bihac had not been occupied by Republika Srpska at that time, so of course we wanted to reach our own territory where we could be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1012, please. And I'll also be asking him to look briefly at P1059, if it's easier to get them both out at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This report -- this is a report signed by Vinko Kondic, and it's entitled "Information on the work and activities of the Kljuc SJB during combat activities on the territory of Kljuc municipality," and it's dated simply Kljuc July 1992. If you could go, please, to section 6.7, which I think is on page 11 of the original. There should be a heading there under 7 "Use of our forces." If you look at the second paragraph of that heading, it states: "The actions by the 30th Division units, together with the Kljuc SJB forces were fast, vigorous, and effective. The resistance of the extremists and fundamentalists was broken. They suffered substantial casualties and some materiel assets used in the armed resistance were destroyed. In the combat operations that took place in the next few days, Milorad Markovic, a military policeman, was killed during the mop-up of Gornji Prhovo and Brane Davic, a civilian, died in the Skrbici Hamlet and Pistanica village." Is that what it says in the original which is before you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with Vinko Kondic's assessment that the actions by the 30th Division, together with the Kljuc SJB forces were fast, vigorous, and effective and that the resistance was quickly broken?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, but I do not agree that we were extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you also agree that the resistance forces of which you were part suffered substantial casualties in the next few days after the operation started on the 28th, as you state?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I disagree. First of all, the forces who were putting up resistance had left for Bihac, which means that there was no resistance. He says it was a fast and vigorous reaction. Those were Serb soldiers attacking unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this time, when you were in the woods, when you were trying to make to Hripavac though, you were with other armed men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were part of a resistance at that point; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We were not a resistance. We were merely providing security for the civilians there. There was no resistance, because they left us in peace for two days to decide whether we would surrender or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, then, as -- do you agree that, however you prefer to characterise your group, that you and the men around you suffered substantial casualties during this period when you were trying to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: During our withdrawal, we did not suffer a single casualty, at least no casualty who was armed. All of those people were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that around the 30th of May, in your statement, you and the men with you made a decision to surrender. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why was that decision made?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We were trying to join forces with the other municipalities: Sanski Most and the rest of them, in order to try and break through in the direction of Bihac. But as that had been all over by that time, we decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, were other groups of people who had been trying to flee at this point surrendering as well? Was there a large-scale surrender at the end of May?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was before I decided to surrender, with other 17 persons. Other groups had surrendered before us, and they were taken to the school, where we eventually surrendered, and then on to Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P936, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're being shown a regular combat report to the command of the 30th Infantry Division. It's headed "Command post of the 1st Infantry Brigade, Sipovo command post, military secret, strictly confidential. Date, 30 of May, 1992. Strictly confidential. Number 1-131/92." If you'd turn to page 2, please. And if I have the correct section, section 3, just above section 3, there is a paragraph which states: "In the Velagici, Kula-Pudin Han area, the 3rd Battalion is conducting mopping up of Green Berets who are surrendering in droves. Some of the Green Berets have fled and are in hiding. One of our soldiers was killed." Is that an accurate statement that people were surrendering in droves around the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I think on the 29th, when this was written, I think the people from Velagici had surrendered before that time. So not on the 29th, but rather immediately after the Serb army arrived in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you read this statement, in this area, do you agree, though, that, if you know, in general, were Muslim men who had fled into the forest surrendering in droves? Is that an accurate assessment?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a correct estimate, because in the village of Velagici, people who were later to disappear in the old school building had indeed surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P654, pleas please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps command, confidential. It is numbered 44-1/157, dated 1st of June, 1992. It is to the Serbian Republic of BH army Main Staff, as it is headed, and it is signed by General Momir Talic. If you could read the last sentence of section 2. The translation, that reads: "In the area of Kljuc and Sanski Most there have been no major changes since the last report. The search of the terrain and seizure of weapons is continuing." Next section of report, section 3, entitled "Situation on the ground," the third sentence reads: "The areas of Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most are under the control of our units." Is that what it states in your original as well?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that by June 1st the area of Kljuc was under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps and that the search and seizure of weapons was continuing? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By the 1st of June, everything was under their control, but they weren't looking for weapons. They were looting and they were taking away prominent people from our villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then by the 1st of June, any form of armed resistance or attempt to leave the area and make it to Bihac was finished; is that right, according to this order?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those people who had left for Bihac must have reached Bihac by that time, I think. In my village, in Pudin Han, I stayed behind, with ten elderly or disabled people, and the others were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's talk now about your decision to surrender. You said in your statement that you and your group decided to surrender and walked to Kljuc. Can you tell me about that journey to Kljuc to surrender and who was with you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't list all the names, but Velid Ticevic was there, policeman Hamdija Kumalic, that's ex-policeman Hamdija Kumalic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't need to know all the names. If you can just tell me how many people there were and whether you knew these people, whether they were from your village. That's what I meant. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There were about 17 people in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you get to Kljuc to surrender? If you can just briefly tell me what happened.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Pero Bajic, a bus driver, came to our village and rounded up the people, telling the people to surrender, and also he told the people who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wanted to go on foot that no one would hurt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you began walking towards Kljuc with a white flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The man in front carried a white flag as a sign of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You started, I think, to tell us that you went to a school earlier. Which school was it that you walked to in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Nikola Mackic Elementary School.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened to you and the group you were with when you arrived at that school?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the school, a double line of people had been formed, through which we had to pass; that is, we had to run the gauntlet. They were holding on to various poles, truncheons, batons, cables, and we had to run between them before entering the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who were these people? Were they soldiers, policemen, civilians, who you had to -- who you had to run between?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly reserve soldiers, ordinary soldiers, civilians, policemen. They were all there to witness what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened when you ran through this gauntlet, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They beat us, whatever they could get hold of. If someone fell, then he would be kicked and beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did that beating end? How did it stop?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It didn't stop. I told you that I was released with ten elderly and sick people, as someone with no guilt, and I was released home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're jumping ahead a little bit. I'm talking now about you going into the school. You've told us you were beaten on the way into the school. Now I want to talk about what happened inside of the school. In your statement you talked about a Serb policeman that you know named Dragan Stojcic.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Dragan Stojcic. He was a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me what he did when he saw you at the school, if you saw him there.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him. First, as we entered, we saw some other people from other villages. The hall was bloodstained. They were sitting with their arms raised, with the three-finger sign, and they had to sing their songs. So that we sat down too and waited to see what would happen. After a while, Mr. Stojcic came in, and he cursed them and said, "Why are you beating these people?" And he chased them all out. However, as soon as he left the hall, they started doing the same again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said "the people in the hall." Were those -- what type of people were they who were being held in the hall? Just if you can be clear. Were those men, women, children, soldiers, civilians? If you can describe the people in the hall.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: They were all civilians. I can describe. They were beaten up. Some of them had blood on them. Some -- actually, in that very hall, a policeman was beaten up who had left the Autonomous Krajina, Hamdija Kumalic. They beat him so badly that he lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many -- and these civilians were Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: He was of Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But in general, just to be clear for the record, the civilians being held in the school hall were not Serb civilians; is that right or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many of these civilians were being held in the hall, if you can remember, approximately?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can say very roughly that there were between 300 and 400 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was guarding these people, including yourself, who were held there, once you were inside of the school?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We were guarded by the reserve policemen, the regular policemen, and interrogators who interrogated us were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you personally interrogated?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe your interrogation, please? Who interrogated you, and what types of questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated by a certain Mr. Tepic. I don't know his first name, but he worked in the department for ID cards. He asked who had weapons, whether I had participated in spreading fear, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you beaten while you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to see, hear, or otherwise tell whether anybody else was being beaten while they were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw many who were interrogated before me, and they were bloodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long were you held in that room, in the gym in the school?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I was held there, together with these ten elderly people, for about five hours, so that about 9.00 p.m. we were taken to a special room. We were given certain certificates saying that we were innocent and that we would be allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Shall I continue, Your Honour, or are we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have a 20-minute break, resuming just before a quarter to 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before we broke, you told us how you and some elderly or ill man who had been held in the school, Nikola Mackic school, were given certificates allowing you to go home. Do you know what happened to the other several hundred people who were held there in the school? Was everybody allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: No. They gave these ten people and me certificates for freedom of movement. We were released at 6.00 a.m., and the others who stayed in the school were taken to camps, either in Bosanska Gradiska or Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you had surrendered. You had left into the woods and you had been armed at one point. Why were you given a certificate to return home instead of being sent to Manjaca? Do you have any explanation for that, why you were given a certificate and others were not?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Once you were released, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I went to my village in Pudin Han, or Donji Hadzici, because one of the detainees who had sick parents, especially his mother, couldn't see well, and his father was seriously ill, so he asked me to take care of them until he came back. Of course, he hoped he would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is this the house of Ibrahim and Fata Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was at Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village is called Donji Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, once you went to the village, I'd like to know if you could tell us a little bit about the work obligation which you were required to take part in once you had been released. In your statement you talk about how had you were told to report for work and you would have to work each day. Can you tell me how soon it was that you began reporting for work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that that day when we arrived at Pudin Han, their checkpoints were there. There was one in Nisret Draganovic's, with 20 or 30 soldiers, and they came to see us and told us that we had to report to them every day, so that they would know that we wouldn't go into the woods to take food to our people and that they would introduce labour obligation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So is it safe to say that at this point the entire area, as far as you could tell, as we saw in one of those documents, was under the control of the VRS and the Kljuc local police forces?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just so I understand you, every morning you would be required to report to this checkpoint and receive instructions?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was the youngest, and they reckoned I was healthier than the others, they designated me as a representative who would have to go to their checkpoint every morning, and they would give me duties: To cut the grass, to carry furniture for their soldiers when they came to the houses to take the furniture away, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as specifically as you can remember, who would assign you your duties every morning? Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There was Ratko Marcetic from Sanski Most. He was a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And describe some of your work details. As part of your work obligation, were you required to go back into the village of Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Once we completed our work duty, we would return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is whether you worked in the village of Pudin Han. In your statement you discuss that you had to work there on occasion.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did all kinds of work. We had to bury the people who had been killed, the civilians, and the animals also who had died, and then there was food in freezers, because there was no electricity. It went bad. So we had to carry that and bury it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, earlier you talked about those people who had been trying to flee in a tractor, and you named some of them who were hit by a shell and killed, and you said that you buried them. Is this what you're referring to, that you buried those people as part of your work detail?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we buried them and others, like Refik Draganovic, Ivan Blazevic, whose throat was slit, and others who were hit by shells. So we buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your best estimate, how many people did you personally take part in helping to bury in those days after you were released from the school in Kljuc? And I'm talking about in the village of Pudin Han.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I personally buried - and I will tell you later - Refik Draganovic, near his house; Ivan Buljan; and I helped with some other civilians in the tractor, the civilians from the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were doing these different types of tasks that you were assigned to do as part of the work obligation -- let me step back. Was this in any way voluntary on your part? Did you have any choice as to whether to perform this work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We had to do what we were told by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were working in Pudin Han, did you notice any looting at all?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was looting. I mentioned it. As a soldier would come with a rifle, or drunk, and he would take a liking to something, a piece of furniture, he would pick it up and we had to load it on to a truck for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You would personally have to load items onto trucks for soldiers who arrived in Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I had to load some things from my own house, that is, the house of my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you can give us an idea how widespread was this? Was this just a couple of incidents that you observed? Was this happening all over the place? Did you see it five times, ten times? Give us an idea of the scale of this looting.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: The looting was on an enormous scale. At first it was more valuable technical appliances, money, jewellery. After that came furniture, the more valuable pieces. And this happened throughout the time I was there in detention, so that at the end they would start taking off tiles from houses and building material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be given P660, please. And while they're getting that, let me ask you:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you saw soldiers doing looting. Was it only soldiers or did you see anybody else committing the crime of looting at that time?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: There were civilians of Serb ethnicity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a look at that document, please. This is a regular combat report. It's headed "1st Krajina Corps command, operative is struck out. Strictly confidential, number 44-1/162. Dated the 4th of June, 1992." And this is signed for General Talic. It is to the Main Staff. If you could read section 3, please. Actually, just the last sentence of section 3.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, talking there about the crisis areas, including Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Donji Vakuf, under the control of 1KK units. And the statement is made: "That the corps command is taking all available measures to prevent various forms of crimes, especially the looting of material goods." Could you please describe to us any and all actions taken by soldiers you saw to prevent looting.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: No measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1046, please. This is a report headed: "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Interior, Banja Luka Security Service Centre, public security station Kljuc, number 17/92, date 28 September 1992. Strictly confidential. Official secret." And it is a report on crimes committed in the municipality from the outbreak of the armed uprising on 27 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look -- let's see if I can figure it out on your page. There's a one-sentence paragraph towards probably the bottom of your page. Sorry, it's on the second page of yours, I guess. Which reads: "There has lately been widespread looting of abandoned Muslim houses." Below that is the statement: "Information collected through intelligence work reveals that the perpetrators were in uniform; that is, they were military persons outside the authority of the SJB. However, because of wartime conditions, military security organs seldom disclose the identity of perpetrators, and punish such acts by sending them to the first front line. Such crimes are reported to the station, which simply does not know how to deal with them." My question is: As far as you know, does that seem accurate to the extent that whether or not you saw the local -- the civilian police taking measures to prevent looting?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: This is not true, because that same civilian police would come to loot. There was a man named Simo. There were other people whose names I didn't know. I knew they were in place of the public security services and I know that they took part in the looting too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1059, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this document before you is headed: "Attention," handwritten at the top, "Attention Colonel Gojko Vujanovic, 1st Krajina Corps Assistant Commander for Civilian Affairs. Confidential. 01-326 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can skip those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a copy of the document -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The copy in English is on the ELMO, Usher? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 2 of the English version, and I think it's probably on page 2 of the original, is the heading: "The onset of the war in the Kljuc area." If you can find that.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The second paragraph under that heading reads: "Individuals and small and large groups of people began illegally appropriating Muslim property in Muslim villages and hamlets during combat operations in the local communes of Velagici, Sanica, Humici, and Peci, and continued to do so when the operations ended. This was done by military personnel, members of the police, and the local Serbs. Later, acts of unlawful appropriation spread like an epidemic. This certainly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened, although such acts have not been typical of the Serbian people throughout its history. There were cases of appropriation of cattle or buying them for next to nothing and taking away all other movable property." Now, from what you stated, is that a fairly accurate assessment of the situation during and immediately after 27 May 1992 in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Other than -- well, other than the problem of looting, can you just tell us briefly what life was like in Kljuc for the Muslim population and Croat population that remained in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult. Uniformed people came, civilians came. They threatened us, they beat us. They were looking for money or gold. They were verbally abusing us. It was a very difficult situation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said in your statement that there were murders, looting, and rapes in the municipality. Does that about sum it up?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as a result of that, what did the people who were remaining there do? Did they want to stay there or did they try to leave? What was the response of the Muslim and Croat population, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that many of the people who had stayed behind, in the former Yugoslavia, they worked hard to earn themselves a decent life, and of course they were sad to be made to leave. And the elderly people who were there were very difficult to convince that they were now supposed to leave. They sometimes preferred dying to leaving their property behind, and they were being compelled to leave their property behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown P989. And this is the book of minutes from sessions of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask you to try to find the minutes from the 6th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's page 13 of the English version, Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it's 00578865 is the ERN of the B/C/S, if I'm correct. Sorry, 3865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not correct, Mr. Nicholls. It's 00573869.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these are the minutes from the Kljuc municipality Crisis Staff session of the 6th of June, 1992. And one of the agenda items, if you start reading down, before we get to the 9th of June meeting, the third from the bottom of the list is that the matter of the organised removal of the Muslim population should be resolved. Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the thing with resolving and unity, which number is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let me help you. Do you have before you page with a reference number 00573869? Moving to the next one, 00573870?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First half of the page, four lines or five lines up. There are several points which are bulleted, and this is the third one before the last. I can't read it myself because I can't recognise the handwriting or the language, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for helping me find that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, does it -- just to be clear, because this is handwriting, and it may be difficult, does it say: "The matter of the organised removal of the Muslim population should be resolved"?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about how people were trying to leave and that older people wanted to stay and had to try to be persuaded to leave. Can you comment on this Crisis Staff entry from the same period, which talks about an organised removal of the Muslim population? From what you could see, was the removal organised or was it not organised in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I think the removal was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And why do you say that? Why do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Because I was one of those whose removal was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, why is -- what was organised about your removal?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, the elderly and sick people, as well as women and children, were leaving. Men of military age were not allowed to leave. First they were made to go to the municipal building to pay their dues, if any outstanding, to the Republika Srpska. After that they were made sign over their property to Republika Srpska of their own free will, and afterwards they would be given documents, using which they could get bus tickets issued to them so they could leave the area and go to a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you personally required to sign documents such as these before you left?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you allowed to bring any -- well, what personal property were you allowed to bring with you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't bring anything, only what I was wearing at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let's go back a little bit to what I think are the reasons that you left. Can you tell us, please, about what happened that you know of Latif Draganovic and his wife in August 1992, and I think this occurred in Hadzici, near where you were living.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Latif Draganovic was a man aged about 70. He was disabled. He had a bad leg, and he was using a crutch to walk. I think his wife's name was Sevle. I'm a bit ashamed to say this, especially of an older woman, but she was a bit of a nut case, you know, slightly deaf, and generally incapable. They lived about 20 metres from my house. Their son was a butcher. He used to be a rich man before the war. His name was Muho and he was a butcher. So I think they were killed because of the money, because they thought that Muho had left them some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who is "they" who thought -- can you just describe in a little bit of detail that killing, what you observed or heard and who, to your knowledge, committed that crime?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the person's name, for the sake of that person's own safety. He was in the Serb army and he is a friend of mine. But Slavko Jandric and Marko Timarac were the killers, and the third man, his nickname was Zobonja. I didn't know his real name, but his nickname was Zobonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you recognised these men when they arrived at the Draganovic house?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for clarity, were all three of these men, the killers, as far as you know, were they members of the armed forces, of the VRS? You said that one of them was.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All three were members. They were guards at a checkpoint in Donji Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This was sometime in August of 1992, I think. If you can just tell us, very briefly, what happened.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We were not allowed to move about in the evening. At dusk we had to be in our homes. Sometimes we would peer out of the window. And I saw those three men who were headed for that house. So when those people were killed, we were called in the morning, as locals, and we were asked who we thought might have done that. Then I saw Mr. Draganovic. He had a number of wounds all over his body. And his wife - my apologies - did not have her underwear on. Of course, she had been raped, and her dress had ripped to pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What kind of -- well, let me stop you. You -- were you -- did you make a formal statement about what you had seen of this crime? What did you tell the police had happened? Were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: We were not allowed to say anything, for our own safety. There were two of their military policemen there to file a report to find out who had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I understand you, even though you had recognised who these men were who you thought you had seen go to the house just before this crime was committed, you did not feel safe in giving those names to the local police, or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sometime later, about a month later, a similar crime occurred at the house you were living at; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Not in that house but the house below, where we all had to assemble at night to sleep there. It was Ramiz Draganovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me about those murders, if you remember when they occurred and how -- what you remember happening that night?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim, Fata Draganovic and myself slept in Ramiz Draganovic's house, with other four or five families. They told us at the checkpoint that this was for the sake of our own personal safety and they could keep an eye on us. They could continue to do their work, and that's why they kept us in one house. They came at about half past 10.00. They said -- they were soldiers from the checkpoint and they were there to make sure that everything was all right. And they took myself and Ibrahim Draganovic outside. First there was Ibrahim and I was behind him. They told us to bring with us our certificates for freedom of movement. But when the two of us got down, they asked Ibrahim for money. He told them that he had no money on him, that they might as well kill him because he had no money. So it was a sort of a tug of war for about five minutes and he was hit by a soldier. A soldier hit him with a rifle and started shooting. I don't know even now how I stayed alive. Ibrahim lay on top of me until about 4.00 in the morning, half past 3.00 in the morning. I was not supposed to contact anyone. I didn't know how much time had elapsed. But later on Fata and the other people in the house told me later on that he had spent about five or six hours lying on top of me. So around 4.30 in the morning I washed the blood off my body and I went to the checkpoint to report what had happened. When I pushed Ibrahim's body off me, I saw that at 10 or 15 metres from there, underneath a pear tree, Ibrahim Kumalic's body was also lying. He had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you know who the perpetrators of this crime were? Did you recognise them? Did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Bajic, son of Pero, bus driver, his brother, his last name was also Bajic. I didn't know his first name and there was also Milan Lukic, son of Mara and Nikica. Mara was an elementary school teacher, my teacher too. And Nikica worked at a ticket office in Kljuc. He was selling bus tickets. And there was a relative of theirs from Humici whose name I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just -- you said they said they were soldiers. Do you know whether or not these men were in fact soldiers in the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that they never went to the front. They just wore uniforms and went around the villages looting. There were neighbours of ours and they knew exactly who had what in terms of material possessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just so I'm clear, how many victims were there of this I guess you would call it an attempted robbery? How many people were killed that night? I think you've said two people.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Two Ibrahims, Kumalic and Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened the next morning when you went to report this crime at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Marjanovic, Mico Marjanovic, who was in charge of the checkpoint, came there, and several soldiers, too and they called the military police in to investigate the scene. Mladen, called Marceta, I think that's what the man's name was, came, and a friend of his. I think the name was Kevac. I'm not sure, but the two of them came to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you tell Lieutenant Marjanovic, or Colonel Marjanovic? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Marjanovic. I told him what happened. I told him the truth, and he called the police to investigate. I told him that the two men, both named Ibrahim, had been killed, and that I had been taken outside the house too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did Lieutenant Marjanovic give you any advice - you talk about that in a bit of your statement - about what to say to the police when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to protect Mr. Marjanovic, but if I have to say it, he asked me to please not say in case I knew who had killed those men, because in that case I would be killed the next evening. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1045, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, this is a Kljuc public security station report dated September 8th, 1992, concerning crimes committed in the municipality of Kljuc area from the start -- from 27th of May, 1992 on. It's signed by Chief Vinko Kondic and it's going to the Banja Luka office. Now, without going all through it, this report talks about the offences of murder being committed against Muslims. It states that looting has taken place of houses abandoned by Muslims on a "massive scale." And I'd like you to read the last two paragraphs of the report, and those, if I may read them, state, in relation to the murders and the looting and the other crimes in the report: "Up to now, the station has established and registered a large number of crimes of all sorts but has not filed reports against either," and it's an abbreviation for unknown persons, "nor, in some cases, against known perpetrators. The reason for this is the advisability of publishing these crimes at this particular moment, in the light of the current political situation and pressure from the international community. It is precisely for these reasons that we are sending you this report with a request that you issue instructions to us," meaning the Kljuc police station, "on how to deal with the crimes committed during the war events." Is that what it says in your version, in the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a suspicion that the translation is somewhat faulty, because --

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't make sense to me, when I read: "The reason for this is the advisability of publishing these crimes at this particular moment, in the light..." Advisability?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it should say exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, depending on how you read it, I think the statement -- we would need a native speaker to read the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can read the paragraph and the interpreters can try to translate it, without looking at the English version of P1045.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's the second-to-last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The paragraph which starts with "Stanica," [phoen] and I want you to read, please, sir, the last sentence. Can I ask you to read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason is that it is necessary to publish these crimes at this moment, in the light of the political situation and pressures from the international community. The question is: How advisable is it to do this now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that clears it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it and clears, and I think we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll give you a rest. You'll go -- you'll be accompanied to where you're staying and you will return to this courtroom tomorrow, in the afternoon, and at 2.15 we will resume with your testimony. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Anything before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Just that I'm going to try to finish very quickly, maybe half an hour or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And can I have an estimate of how long you expect your cross to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know that I usually keep it very short. I don't think it would last even an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Do you have the next witness, without mentioning his name, from the Sanski Most, in line for tomorrow, or not? I have been given, or we have been given, a statement of a witness which belongs to the Sanski Most list, whose appearance here was delayed for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know the witness that Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he here in The Hague or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe so. That's not my witness. I've been very inaccurate. I thought this was going to take me much longer, but I think that witness will be ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I did tell the lawyer who was taking that witness that I thought that most of tomorrow would be taken up, but I will try to have that witness ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because as I see it, we might finish with this witness tomorrow by the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I thank you all. Have a nice evening, and we'll resume tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
